facts.statement: Galahadosuchus lived during the Late Triassic, specifically the Carnian to Rhaetian stages.
facts.quote: Age: Late Triassic (Carnian–Rhaetian)

facts.statement: The type locality of Galahadosuchus is Cromhall Quarry.
facts.quote: Type locality: Cromhall Quarry

facts.statement: Galahadosuchus fossils were found in the United Kingdom.
facts.quote: Country: United Kingdom

facts.statement: Galahadosuchus is classified as a member of the order Crocodylomorpha and the family Saltoposuchidae.
facts.quote: A member of Crocodylomorpha belonging to the family Saltoposuchidae.

facts.statement: The only known species of Galahadosuchus is G. jonesi.
facts.quote: species: jonesi

facts.statement: Galahadosuchus is an extinct saltoposuchid crocodylomorph found in Late Triassic fissure deposits in the United Kingdom.
facts.quote: Galahadosuchus is an extinct genus of saltoposuchid crocodylomorph from the Late Triassic fissure deposits of Cromhall Quarry in the United Kingdom.

facts.statement: The known remains of Galahadosuchus include a partial postcranial skeleton with most hindlimbs, an almost complete forelimb, and tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: It is known from a partial postcranial skeleton including most of the hindlimbs, an almost complete forelimb and a series of tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: Galahadosuchus was a gracile animal characterized by long, slender limbs.
facts.quote: Based on these remains Galahadosuchus was a gracile animal with long, slender limbs.

facts.statement: Galahadosuchus is considered a terrestrial quadruped with an erect, digitigrade stance adapted for a fast-running lifestyle.
facts.quote: Like many other early crocodylomorphs it is considered to have been a terrestrial quadruped, showing evidence of an erect, digitigrade stance and adaptations towards a cursorial lifestyle.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Galahadosuchus was recovered by Ron Croucher in 1969.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Galahadosuchus, NHMUK PV R 10002, was recovered by Ron Croucher in 1969

facts.statement: The holotype was found at site 1 of the fissure deposits at Cromhall Quarry in Gloucestershire, southwest England.
facts.quote: from site 1 of the fissure deposits at Cromhall Quarry in Gloucestershire, southwest England.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen consists of a partially articulated postcranial skeleton, a nearly complete right forelimb, isolated bones like osteoderms and ribs, and the remains of a rhynchocephalian reptile.
facts.quote: The specimen is preserved across two slabs and consists of a partially articulated postcranial skeleton including parts of the tail and hindlimbs, a nearly complete right forelimb, several isolated elements such as osteoderms, ribs and non-caudal vertebrae as well as the remains of a rhynchocephalian reptile.

facts.statement: Cromhall Quarry, also known as Slickstones Quarry, is a Late Triassic to Early Jurassic fissure deposit in the Bristol Channel area.
facts.quote: The Cromhall Quarry, also known as Slickstones Quarry, is one of several Late Triassic to Early Jurassic fissure fill deposits in the Bristol Channel area

facts.statement: Distinguishing features of Galahadosuchus include relatively short and stout ulnare and radiale proximal carpal bones, which exceed a quarter of their maximum length.
facts.quote: Among the distinguishing features of this genus are the relatively short and stout ulnare and radiale, the proximal carpal bones, who′s with exceeds a quarter of their maximum length.

facts.statement: In Galahadosuchus, the proximal carpal bones are at most one-tenth the length of their respective paired limb bones in the forearm.
facts.quote: Each bone is at most only a tenth the length of their respective limb bone pairing in the forearm, i.e. radius plus humerus for the radiale and ulna plus humerus for the ulnare.

facts.statement: The back of Galahadosuchus was covered by a double row of paramedian osteoderms, similar to other early crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: As in most other early crocodylomorphs the back of Galahadosuchus was covered by what a double-row of paramedian osteoderms.

facts.statement: The individual osteoderms of Galahadosuchus are elongated, being 2.5 times longer than they are wide.
facts.quote: The individual bony plates are elongated, 2.5 times longer than wide

facts.statement: The osteoderms of Galahadosuchus are described as leaf-shaped or subrectangular with a straight medial edge and a curved outer edge ending in a spike-like process.
facts.quote: Their shape is described as "leaf-shaped" or subrectangular, featuring a straight medial edge where each osteoderm meets its partner and a curved outer edge that flows into a spike-like process towards the front.

facts.statement: The surface of Galahadosuchus osteoderms is ornamented with shallow pits surrounding a long midline keel.
facts.quote: The surface is ornamented by a pattern of shallow pits that surround a long keel that runs down the osteoderms midline.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses by Bodenham and colleagues recovered Galahadosuchus as a member of the family Saltoposuchidae.
facts.quote: Both phylogenetic analysis run by Bodenham and colleagues recovered Galahadosuchus as a member of the family Saltoposuchidae

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses found Galahadosuchus to be the sister taxon of Terrestrisuchus.
facts.quote: in both instances it was found to be the sister taxon of Terrestrisuchus from the nearby Pant-y-Ffynnon Quarry.

facts.statement: It is debated whether different weighting methods in phylogenetic analysis affect the placement of Galahadosuchus within the family Saltoposuchidae.
facts.quote: Extended implied weighting meanwhile recovered different results based on the used k-value.

facts.statement: Galahadosuchus is interpreted as a small, slender terrestrial quadruped with an erect posture.
facts.quote: Like other small, slender early crocodylomorphs including the closely related Terrestrisuchus, Galahadosuchus has been interpreted as a terrestrial, possibly cursorial quadruped with an erect posture.

facts.statement: Elongated proximal carpals in Galahadosuchus formed a single functional unit adapted to bear the animal's weight.
facts.quote: The elongated proximal carpals of early crocodylomorphs are thought to be an adaptation to bearing the animal′s weight, forming a single functional unit.

facts.statement: The shortened first metacarpal suggests the corresponding digit did not bear weight when Galahadosuchus was on the ground.
facts.quote: The shortened first metacarpal seen in both Galahadosuchus and Terrestrisuchus likely means that the matching digit was likewise shorter, something which has been interpreted as a sign that this particular finger did not bear the animal′s weight when on the ground.

facts.statement: A greater metatarsal to femur ratio suggests Galahadosuchus may have been a faster runner than its sister taxon.
facts.quote: Finally the greater metatarsal to femur ratio may mean that Galahadosuchus was a faster runner than its sister taxon.

facts.statement: The holotype of Galahadosuchus jonesi is specimen NHMUK PV R 10002.
Galahadosuchus was described from a semi-articulated partial postcranial skeleton found at Cromhall Quarry in the Bristol Channel area.
Galahadosuchus lived in the Late Triassic fissure deposits of the Bristol Channel area in southwest England and south Wales.
Galahadosuchus is classified within the clade Saltoposuchidae and is the sister taxon to Terrestrisuchus.
Galahadosuchus is a new genus and species named Galahadosuchus jonesi.
The fifth metacarpal of Galahadosuchus was less developed than in Terrestrisuchus and resembled the first digit.
facts.quote: The fifth metacarpal of Galahadosuchus is not as well developed as its counterpart in Terrestrisuchus, instead bearing closer resemblance to the first digit.

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether the humerus proportions indicate Galahadosuchus was less capable of terrestrial movement, noting potential dataset biases from including modern crocodiles.
facts.quote: Similarly, the fact that the humerus does not contribute as much to the forelimbs as in Terrestrisuchus could be interpreted as a sign of the animal being less capable of terrestrial movement based on prior studies, but again the team that described Galahadosuchus raised the caveat that the used dataset might be influenced by the inclusion of modern crocodiles with their generally sprawling rather than erect posture.

facts.statement: The interpretation that the shortened first digit did not bear weight in Galahadosuchus is based on the shortened first metacarpal.
facts.quote: The shortened first metacarpal seen in both Galahadosuchus and Terrestrisuchus likely means that the matching digit was likewise shorter, something which has been interpreted as a sign that this particular finger did not bear the animal′s weight when on the ground.
